extracted.intended_audience: writers, poets, dramatists, and public speakers; students of rhetoric and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing and judging 'the sublime' in literature and rhetoric (especially poetry, tragedy, and oratory), with specific criteria, sources of greatness, and common faults to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy spoiled by vulgar acting
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular condemnation that tragedy can be and often is spoilt by the stupid vulgarity of actors (their overacting, poses, or representations of characters unsuitable to their social status).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a criticism of acting, not of the poetry itself; poor acting (e.g., over-gesturing, vulgar attitudes) can make excellent poetry appear inferior. Examples: Callippides called 'the monkey' for overacting; criticisms apply when actors present women who are not ladies. The refutation: tragedy's quality can be gauged by reading aloud — it must not depend solely on performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability/gauging quality by reading aloud
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy fulfils its function even without acting and its quality can be gauged by reading the text aloud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a tragedy is aesthetically successful, its effect should persist in the purely literary/rhetorical form; therefore a play should work when read, not only when staged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle and music as added elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy contains in addition to epic elements a considerable element of its own in spectacle and music, which make the pleasure more vivid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements augment vividness and can be effective whether read or acted; they are distinguishing features that contribute to tragedy's greater immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of length and unity of action (tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy attains its end with greater economy of length; concentration is more effective than what is spread over a long period. Epic tends to have less unity because it comprises several separate actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A concentrated single action gives stronger artistic effect; if an epic compresses one plot to the scale of a tragedy it may seem curtailed, or if it conforms to epic length it may feel thin and diluted. Aim for unity and appropriate economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy's artistic function: produce specific pleasure (catharsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedies should produce a particular pleasurable effect — the release (or 'relief') of pity and fear and related emotions (what later critics call catharsis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The criterion for judging tragedy is whether it attains the pleasure it is meant to produce (i.e., the emotional purification/release), not merely entertainment or spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity defined as consummate excellence and distinction of language
rubrics_metrics.description: The sublime consists in a consummate excellence and distinction of language that transports the audience out of themselves; it inspires wonder and exerts irresistible power rather than mere persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublime passages should elevate and transport readers/listeners, leaving a sense of wonder and an indelible impression. The effect is not simply to convince but to move and astonish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime's sudden flash vs gradual craft
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-timed flash of sublimity can reveal the speaker's power at a single stroke, scattering everything before it like lightning, while inventive skill and marshalling of facts usually emerge gradually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft both gradual composition and the ability to produce singular sublime moments; a single luminous passage can show genius as effectively as sustained invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate art to shape natural genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Although genius is natural, art (rules, practice, and judgement) is needed to determine degree, timing, and safe practice; art curbs and refines nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reject rules as constraining genius; learn rules of practice to avoid excesses and to hit the 'happy moment' reliably. Experience and method improve the application of natural talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tumidity (bombast / misplaced tumidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tumidity — empty inflation, pomp, bombast — arises when writers aiming at grandeur overshoot and become ridiculous or trivial rather than sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: exaggerated conceits (e.g., calling Xerxes 'the Persian Zeus'), inflated metaphors (vultures as 'living sepulchres'), overblown phrasing that provokes laughter. Tumidity produces the opposite of the intended effect and should be guarded against; writers often err trying to avoid being feeble and thereby become bombastic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid puerility (frigid over-subtlety)
rubrics_metrics.description: Puerility is the opposite fault of tumidity: an over-subtle, mean-spirited, or affected delicacy that results in frigid failure and trivial conceits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: excessive refinement or prettiness that aims to please but results in tinsel affectation. Writers fall into this by over-elaboration and trying to be exquisite; avoid contrived cleverness that lacks true emotional power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Parenthyrson (misplaced or excessive emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parenthyrson: emotion misplaced or pointless where none is needed, or unrestrained where restraint is required — emotional outbursts that the subject does not warrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such uncontrolled emotion appears unseemly to an audience that does not share the emotion and makes the passage tedious; emotional passages require proportion and appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid frigidity (cold conceits / insincere novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frigidity is dryness, pedantry, or an obsession with strange conceits and novelty that produce puerile or trivial effects rather than grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Timaeus's odd comparisons and Xenophon's awkward conceits. The fault stems from a passion for novelty; avoid forced wit and trivial conceits that undermine weight and seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: True sublimity endures and supplies 'food for thought'
rubrics_metrics.description: A truly sublime passage leaves abundant material for reflection: its effect is stubborn and indelible, outlasting the initial utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test: if a well-versed reader after repeated attention finds a passage loses effect or sinks in esteem, it is not truly sublime. Grand style should continue to yield thought and pleasure on reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek universal appeal where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: What is truly beautiful and sublime pleases all people at all times; unanimity across differing ages, tastes, and habits is a strong test of sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If diverse judges across time and circumstance agree on the greatness of a passage, that unanimity strengthens the claim to sublimity. Aim for elements that transcend narrow fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five sources of the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: The five principal sources: (1) command of full-blooded ideas; (2) inspiration of vehement emotion; (3) proper construction of figures (figures of thought and figures of speech); (4) nobility of phrase (choice of words, use of metaphor and poetic ornament); (5) the general effect of dignity and elevation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two (full ideas and vehement emotion) are largely natural; the other three are partly matters of art. Analyze and cultivate each source: generate rich ideas, marshal genuine emotion, use figures properly, choose noble phrasing, and shape the overall dignified effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of full-blooded ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Full-blooded ideas — weighty, robust, and substantial conceptions — are a primary source of sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop content that is substantial and thought-provoking; avoid airy or trivial matter. (Listed as one of the five sources of the sublime.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspiration of vehement emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Vehement, genuine emotion supplies power to sublime expression; emotion is a major source but not identical with sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotion must be appropriate and genuine; distinguish heartfelt vehemence that uplifts from mere rant or misplaced passion (see Parenthyrson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of figures (figures of thought and speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: The correct construction and deployment of rhetorical figures — both figures of thought and figures of speech — contributes to sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures must serve the idea and the emotion; misuse or excessive ornamentation leads to tumidity or puerility. Arrange words and clauses (composition/arrangement) to produce a grand total effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nobility of phrase: choice of words, metaphor, ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Nobility of phrase — the selection of elevated diction, apt metaphor, and tasteful poetic ornament — is essential to grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on diction and imagery: choose words and metaphors that lift rather than flatter; poetic ornament should add to dignity, not to bombast.

rubrics_metrics.name: General effect: dignity and elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: The encompassing effect of dignity and elevation, synthesizing the other sources, is itself a source of sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft the overall tone and cumulative impression so that the whole passage communicates grandeur and weight; this gestalt is as important as individual devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware excessive novelty and conceits
rubrics_metrics.description: A passion for novel ideas and strange conceits can produce literary weeds — faults arising from the craze for novelty which undermines true greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty can contribute to success but also to failure; limit 'strange conceits' and forced originality that distracts from substance and dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary judgement develops from experience and study
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgement in literature is the last fruit of ripe experience; discernment in sublime matters may be derived from practice, study, and the art's prescriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on natural instinct; cultivate judgement through reading, imitation of great models, and mindful practice of the art's rules about degree, timing, and restraint.
